categories.name: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
Government and the law in Australia

questions.text: Who are Australia's first inhabitants?
options: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are Australia's first inhabitants and have the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world.

questions.text: Where are Torres Strait Islander peoples traditionally from?
options: Islands between northern Queensland and Papua New Guinea
questions.explanation: Torres Strait Islander peoples are from islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.

questions.text: When did the First Fleet arrive from Great Britain?
questions.explanation: The First Fleet arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788.

questions.text: Who was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales?
questions.explanation: Captain Arthur Phillip was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales.

questions.text: What began in 1851 in New South Wales and Victoria?
questions.explanation: A gold rush began in 1851 after gold was discovered in New South Wales and Victoria.

questions.text: Which group was the first large group of migrants to Australia not from Europe?
questions.explanation: Chinese people who arrived during the gold rush were the first large group of migrants not from Europe.

questions.text: When did the separate colonies unite as the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.explanation: The colonies united into the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901.

questions.text: What happened in the 1967 Referendum?
options: Aboriginal peoples were allowed to be counted in official population estimates
questions.explanation: The 1967 Referendum allowed Aboriginal peoples to be counted in official estimates of the Australian population.

questions.text: What is Australia's national language?
questions.explanation: English is Australia's national language and is an important part of national identity.

questions.text: How many states does Australia have?
questions.explanation: Australia has six states.

questions.text: How many mainland territories are listed in the booklet?
questions.explanation: The booklet identifies two mainland territories: the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra is Australia's capital city.

questions.text: What is the capital city of New South Wales?
questions.explanation: Sydney is the capital city of New South Wales.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Victoria?
questions.explanation: Melbourne is the capital city of Victoria.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Queensland?
questions.explanation: Brisbane is the capital city of Queensland.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Perth is the capital city of Western Australia.

questions.text: What is the capital city of South Australia?
questions.explanation: Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Tasmania?
questions.explanation: Hobart is the capital city of Tasmania.

questions.text: What is the capital city of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Darwin is the capital city of the Northern Territory.

questions.text: Who may perform a Welcome to Country?
options: An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region.

questions.text: Who can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country?
questions.explanation: Anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country.

questions.text: On what date is Australia Day celebrated?
questions.explanation: Australia Day is celebrated on 26 January each year.

questions.text: On what date is Anzac Day commemorated?
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April each year.

questions.text: What does Anzac stand for?
options: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
Australian and New Zealand Alliance Council
questions.explanation: Anzac stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.

questions.text: What does the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: The six states and the territories
questions.explanation: The seven points of the Commonwealth Star represent the six states and the territories.

questions.text: What does the Southern Cross on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: A group of stars visible in the southern sky
questions.explanation: The Southern Cross is a group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky.

questions.text: What colour on the Australian Aboriginal Flag represents the earth?
questions.explanation: The red lower half of the Australian Aboriginal Flag represents the earth.

questions.text: What does the white colour on the Torres Strait Islander Flag symbolise?
questions.explanation: The colour white on the Torres Strait Islander Flag symbolises peace.

questions.text: What is Australia's national flower?
questions.explanation: The golden wattle is Australia's national flower.

questions.text: What is Australia's national anthem?
questions.explanation: Advance Australia Fair is Australia's national anthem.

questions.text: What type of democracy does Australia have?
questions.explanation: Australia's system of government is a parliamentary democracy.

questions.text: Where does the power of government come from in Australia?
questions.explanation: The power of government comes from the Australian people because citizens vote for representatives.

questions.text: What does the Rule of Law mean?
options: No person or group is above the law
Religious leaders are above the law
questions.explanation: The Rule of Law means everyone, including people in positions of power, must obey Australian laws.

questions.text: How should change occur in Australia?
options: Through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process
questions.explanation: Australians believe change should occur through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process.

questions.text: How should Australians treat people from different backgrounds?
questions.explanation: Australia's democratic system expects all people to be treated with dignity and respect regardless of background.

questions.text: What does freedom of speech allow people to do?
options: Say and write what they think within the law
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech allows people to express ideas and opinions while obeying Australian law.

questions.text: Can people peacefully criticise the government in Australia?
questions.explanation: People may criticise the government and protest peacefully as long as they obey the law.

questions.text: What does freedom of expression include?
options: Expressing views through art, film, music and literature
Breaking any law for artistic purposes
questions.explanation: Freedom of expression includes expressing views through art, film, music and literature within the law.

questions.text: What is freedom of association?
options: The right to form and join legal associations
The duty to join a political party
The right to join illegal groups
The power to force others to join
questions.explanation: Freedom of association is the right to form and join legal groups or to choose not to join them.

questions.text: Can a person be forced to join an association in Australia?
options: Yes, if it is a political party
Yes, if it is a union
Yes, if the government requests it
questions.explanation: People cannot be forced to join an association.

questions.text: Does Australia have an official national religion?
questions.explanation: Australia has no official national religion.

questions.text: What happens if a religious practice conflicts with Australian law?
options: The person chooses which rule to follow
questions.explanation: Where a religious practice conflicts with Australian law, Australian law prevails.

questions.text: How does Australian law treat citizens of different religions?
options: According to the size of the religion
questions.explanation: The government and the law treat all citizens equally regardless of religion or belief.

questions.text: What does gender equality mean in Australia?
options: Men and women have equal rights
Only men may join the Defence Force
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights and equal access to opportunities in Australia.

questions.text: What does a 'fair go' mean?
options: Achievements should result from talents, work and effort
questions.explanation: A fair go means people should have equal opportunity and succeed through their talents, work and effort.

questions.text: Which is a responsibility of Australian citizens?
options: Serve in the Defence Force full time
questions.explanation: Australian citizens must obey Australia's laws.

questions.text: Which is a responsibility of citizens aged 18 or over?
options: Vote in federal and state or territory elections and referenda
questions.explanation: Voting is a responsibility, right and privilege for Australian citizens aged 18 years or over.

questions.text: What may Australian citizens be called to do in court?
questions.explanation: Citizens on the electoral roll may be called to serve on a jury.

questions.text: Is service in the Australian Defence Force compulsory?
questions.explanation: Service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary, although citizens have a responsibility to defend Australia if needed.

questions.text: Which is a privilege of Australian citizenship?
questions.explanation: Australian citizens may apply for an Australian passport and re-enter Australia freely.

questions.text: Can Australian citizens seek election to parliament?
options: Only if appointed by the King
questions.explanation: Eligible Australian citizens may seek election to parliament.

questions.text: What assistance may an Australian citizen seek while overseas?
options: Consular assistance from an Australian official
questions.explanation: Australian citizens may seek consular assistance from Australian officials while overseas.

questions.text: Can Australian citizens apply for children born overseas to become citizens by descent?
options: Only if the child is over 18
Only if both parents were born in Australia
questions.explanation: Australian citizens can apply for a child born overseas to become an Australian citizen by descent.

questions.text: What is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections?
questions.explanation: Eligible citizens must vote in federal and state or territory elections.

questions.text: What is a referendum?
options: A vote to change the Australian Constitution
questions.explanation: A referendum is a vote on a proposed change to the Australian Constitution.

questions.text: What is jury service intended to help ensure?
options: That the court system is open and fair
questions.explanation: Jury service helps ensure the court system is open and fair.

questions.text: Which statement about freedom of religion is correct?
options: People may follow any religion or no religion
The government chooses a religion for each citizen
questions.explanation: People are free to follow any religion or no religion, but Australian law must be obeyed.

questions.text: Which statement about peaceful protest is correct?
options: It is allowed if it remains within the law
Violence is acceptable if many people agree
questions.explanation: People may protest peacefully, but protests must obey the law and must not injure people or damage property.

questions.text: Are all Australians equal under the law?
options: No, public officials have more rights
Only citizens are equal under the law
questions.explanation: All Australians are equal under the law.

questions.text: What is expected when Australians disagree?
options: They should prevent others from speaking
questions.explanation: Australians believe disagreement should be handled peacefully and with respect.

questions.text: Who conducts federal elections and referendums?
questions.explanation: The Australian Electoral Commission conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the electoral roll.

questions.text: Is the Australian Electoral Commission independent of the government?
questions.explanation: The Australian Electoral Commission is independent of the government.

questions.text: How is voting conducted in Australian elections?
questions.explanation: Voting is by secret ballot, so no one has to know how a person voted.

questions.text: What may happen if a person does not vote without a good reason?
options: They may have to pay a fine
questions.explanation: A person who fails to vote without a good reason may have to pay a fine.

questions.text: When did the Australian Constitution come into effect?
questions.explanation: The Australian Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901.

questions.text: What does the Australian Constitution set out?
options: The basic rules for the government of Australia
questions.explanation: The Australian Constitution sets out the basic rules for the government of Australia.

questions.text: What is required to change the Australian Constitution?
options: A double majority in a referendum
A decision by the Prime Minister alone
A decision by the High Court alone
questions.explanation: A constitutional change requires a national majority and a majority of voters in a majority of states.

questions.text: Which branch of power makes laws?
questions.explanation: Legislative power is the power to make and change laws.

questions.text: Which branch of power puts laws into practice?
questions.explanation: Executive power is the power to put laws into practice.

questions.text: Which branch of power interprets and applies laws?
questions.explanation: Judicial power is exercised by courts and judges to interpret and apply laws.

questions.text: Who is Australia's Head of State?
questions.explanation: The King of Australia is Australia's Head of State.

questions.text: Who represents the King at the federal level?
questions.explanation: The Governor-General represents the King in Australia at the federal level.

questions.text: Who represents the King in each Australian state?
questions.explanation: A Governor represents the King in each state.

questions.text: Who is the leader of the Australian Government?
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister is the leader of the Australian Government.

questions.text: Who leads a state government?
questions.explanation: The Premier leads a state government.

questions.text: Who leads a territory government?
questions.explanation: The Chief Minister leads a territory government.

questions.text: What are the two Houses of the Australian Parliament?
options: The House of Representatives and the Senate
The Cabinet and the High Court
The House of Commons and the Senate
questions.explanation: The Australian Parliament has the House of Representatives and the Senate.

questions.text: What is another name for the House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The House of Representatives is also called the Lower House or the People's House.

questions.text: What is another name for the Senate?
questions.explanation: The Senate is also called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House.

questions.text: How many senators are there in total?
questions.explanation: There are 76 senators in total.

questions.text: How many senators does each state elect?
questions.explanation: Each state elects 12 senators.

questions.text: How many senators does each mainland territory elect?
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory each elect two senators.

questions.text: Who is the leader of a local government?
questions.explanation: A mayor or shire president leads a local government.

questions.text: Which level of government is responsible for immigration and citizenship?
questions.explanation: The Australian Government is responsible for immigration and citizenship.

questions.text: Which level of government is primarily responsible for hospitals and schools?
questions.explanation: State and territory governments are primarily responsible for hospitals, health services and schools.

questions.text: Which level of government is generally responsible for rubbish collection?
questions.explanation: Local governments are generally responsible for rubbish collection.

questions.text: How is the Australian Government generally formed after a federal election?
options: By the party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: The party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives generally forms government.

questions.text: What is a proposed new law called?
questions.explanation: A proposal to introduce a new law or change an existing law is called a Bill.

questions.text: What is Royal Assent?
options: The Governor-General signing a Bill into law
The Prime Minister announcing an election
The High Court reviewing a case
questions.explanation: Royal Assent is given when the Governor-General signs a Bill into law.

questions.text: Who decides whether a person is guilty in a court case?
questions.explanation: The police may investigate and give evidence, but the court decides guilt.

questions.text: What should Australians do under the Rule of Law?
options: Obey the law even when no one is watching
Follow only laws they agree with
Let cultural rules replace Australian law
questions.explanation: Australian values require everyone to obey the law at all times.

questions.text: Why is voting compulsory in Australia?
options: It shows the importance of participating in elections
It allows the government to know each vote
questions.explanation: Compulsory voting reflects the importance of citizens participating in democracy.

questions.text: What is acceptable freedom of speech?
options: Expressing ideas freely within the law
Encouraging others to break the law
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech is protected when exercised within Australian law.

questions.text: Is promoting violence against another person or group acceptable?
options: Yes, if based on political disagreement
questions.explanation: Promoting violence is against Australian values and law.

questions.text: May Australians join or leave legal organisations voluntarily?
questions.explanation: Freedom of association allows people to join or leave legal organisations voluntarily.

questions.text: Can religious law replace Australian law?
options: Yes, if a religious leader agrees
questions.explanation: Religious laws have no legal status over Australian law.

questions.text: Is forced marriage legal in Australia?
questions.explanation: Forced marriage is against the law in Australia.

questions.text: Is polygamy legal in Australia?
questions.explanation: Being married to more than one person at the same time is against Australian law.

questions.text: How should people of different religions be treated?
options: According to the size of their religion
According to the religion of the government
Only citizens should be treated equally
questions.explanation: Australian values require equal treatment regardless of religion or belief.

questions.text: Can two men or two women marry each other under Australian law?
questions.explanation: Under Australian law, two people may marry each other, including two men or two women.

questions.text: Should men and women have equal access to education and employment?
options: Only if they have the same income
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights and should have equal access to education and employment.

questions.text: Can a woman get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills?
questions.explanation: Employment decisions should be based on skills and qualifications, not gender.

questions.text: Can either spouse apply for a divorce?
questions.explanation: Either spouse may apply for divorce even if the other spouse wants to continue the marriage.

questions.text: What does a 'fair go' mean in employment?
options: The best-qualified person should be selected
The wealthiest person should be selected
A citizen should always be selected over a migrant
questions.explanation: A fair go means opportunity should be based on skills, experience and effort.

questions.text: How should Australians respond to disagreement?
questions.explanation: Australians value peaceful disagreement, mutual respect and tolerance.

questions.text: Is violence against a spouse or partner acceptable?
questions.explanation: Physical violence against a spouse or partner is a criminal offence.

questions.text: Should lawful actions of the police be supported?
questions.explanation: Australians are expected to support lawful police actions and obey lawful requests.

questions.text: Does racism have a place in Australia?
questions.explanation: Racism has no place in Australia and can be unlawful.

questions.text: What does mateship mean?
options: Helping each other in times of need
questions.explanation: Mateship means helping and receiving help from others, especially in difficult times.

questions.text: Why is volunteering valued?
options: It strengthens the community and helps people belong
It is compulsory for all citizens
It is only for retired people
questions.explanation: Volunteering supports others, builds skills and strengthens community belonging.

questions.text: What should people living in Australia make an effort to learn?
questions.explanation: English is Australia's national language and an important unifying element of society.

questions.text: Why is learning English important?
options: It helps with education, employment and community participation
It is required to vote in every election
It is only needed for government jobs
questions.explanation: English supports education, work, economic participation and social cohesion.

questions.text: What should a person do if they suspect someone is planning a serious crime?
options: Report it to Australian government authorities
questions.explanation: Helping to keep society safe includes reporting suspected serious crime to authorities.

questions.text: What should a person do if they know a child is being abused?
options: Wait until the child becomes an adult
questions.explanation: Suspected child abuse should be reported to police for investigation.

questions.text: Is sharing sexual photos online without consent acceptable?
options: Yes, if the image was sent privately
Yes, if the person is an adult
Only if no money is involved
questions.explanation: Sharing sexual images without consent can be illegal cyber abuse.

questions.text: Can Australian citizens hold citizenship of another country?
options: Yes, if the other country's laws allow it
questions.explanation: Australian citizens may hold dual or multiple citizenship if the other country's laws permit it.

questions.text: Must an Australian citizen in Australia obey Australian law even if they are also a citizen of another country?
options: Only if they were born in Australia
questions.explanation: All Australian citizens in Australia must obey Australian laws at all times.

questions.text: Can some Australian laws apply to citizens while they are overseas?
questions.explanation: Some Australian laws apply to Australian citizens even when they are overseas.

questions.text: What is expected of people who are able to support themselves and their families?
options: They should try to do so
They should rely entirely on others
questions.explanation: Australians expect people who are able to support themselves and their families to try to do so.

questions.text: What should Australian citizens avoid doing?
questions.explanation: Shared Australian values include loyalty to Australia and not undermining its interests and security.
